posts.title: Tire pressure: where to find the right number and when to check
posts.body:
The right pressure for your tires is the number your vehicle maker sets, not the number printed on the tire. The sidewall shows a maximum, and FuelEconomy.gov says not to inflate to it.

Where to find it: a label on the driver's door edge or door pillar, sometimes in the glove box, and in the owner's manual. It's usually listed in both psi and kPa. The UK Highway Code adds that pressure should match the maker's figure for the load you're carrying.

When to check: NHTSA recommends at least once a month, spare included. The Highway Code says weekly and before a long journey. Check when the tires are cold, after the car has been parked for about three hours, because warm tires give misleading readings.

Why it matters: NHTSA links low pressure to flats, blowouts and tread separation, as well as uneven wear and shorter tire life. FuelEconomy.gov estimates gas mileage drops about 0.2% for every 1 psi below the recommended pressure.

About the warning light: US passenger cars, light trucks and vans have had tire pressure monitoring (TPMS) since the 2008 model year. It only lights up when a tire is significantly low, so it doesn't replace a monthly check. If the light flashes for a minute or so and then stays on, the system itself may have a fault.

Log each check in Checkpit and set a monthly reminder so it doesn't slip.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Tires: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/tires
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code, Annex 6: Vehicle maintenance, safety and security: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/annex-6-vehicle-maintenance-safety-and-security
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp

posts.title: Tire tread depth: legal limits and how to check
posts.body:
Every tire reaches a point where it's worn out, and the limit depends on where you drive.

United States: NHTSA advises replacing tires when the tread is down to 2/32 of an inch (about 1.6 mm).

United Kingdom: cars, light vans and light trailers need at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central three-quarters of the tread, all the way around the tire.

Victoria, Australia: tires need at least 1.5 mm in all principal grooves, and the tread must not wear down to where a wear indicator touches the road. Elsewhere, check your own state or provincial road authority.

How to check: most tires have tread wear indicators, small raised bars inside the grooves. When the tread is level with them, NHTSA says it's time to replace the tire. In the US, NHTSA also describes the penny test: put a penny into a groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. If you can see the top of his head, replace the tire.

While you're there: look for deep cuts, cracks and bulges. Victoria's rules say a tire with damage like that must come off the car, and repairs are only allowed in the tread area, not the sidewall or shoulder. NHTSA suggests checking tread at the same time as pressure, at least once a month.

Note each check in Checkpit so you can see how quickly your tires are wearing.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Tires: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/tires
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code, Annex 6: Vehicle maintenance, safety and security: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/annex-6-vehicle-maintenance-safety-and-security
- Department of Transport and Planning (Victoria), VSI 16 Tyre maintenance and repair: https://transport.vic.gov.au/registration-and-licensing/registration/standard-and-non-standard-vehicle-information/vehicle-standards-information/tyre-maintenance-and-repair

posts.title: Oil changes: how to find the right interval for your car
posts.body:
There's no single oil change interval that fits every car. The right one comes from your vehicle maker, and it can change with how you drive.

Start with the owner's manual or a dealer. They give the interval and the oil type your engine needs. California's used oil program notes that some engines require synthetic oil only.

Oil life monitors: some cars have a monitor that tells you when an oil change is due. If yours does, it's the most direct signal you have.

Normal or severe driving: the maker's standard interval assumes normal driving. California's guidance lists conditions that may mean changing oil more often: very cold or very hot weather, towing or hauling heavy loads, lots of trips under five miles, and a lot of idling or stop-and-go traffic. If any of these is part of a typical week for you, check whether your manual has a separate severe-service schedule.

Use the right grade: FuelEconomy.gov says using the oil grade the maker recommends can improve gas mileage by 1% to 2%, and using a heavier grade than specified, such as 10W-30 in an engine designed for 5W-30, can lower it by 1% to 2%. It also suggests looking for "Energy Conserving" in the API symbol on the bottle.

Log each oil change in Checkpit with the mileage. The app's oil change reminder starts at 6 months or 5,000 miles (8,000 km); change it to match your manual.

Sources:
- CalRecycle (State of California), Check Your Number: https://www2.calrecycle.ca.gov/UsedOil/changeinterval
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp

posts.title: Brake fluid: what it does and when to change it
posts.body:
Brake fluid turns a push on the pedal into stopping power. Pressing the pedal sends fluid from the master cylinder to the pistons that squeeze the pads against the brake discs.

Why it wears out: brake fluid attracts moisture. AAA's brake care guide says not to leave the reservoir open and to throw out spare fluid from an opened bottle. Tesla's owner instructions also say to use only new fluid from a sealed container, because old or opened fluid absorbs moisture and reduces braking performance. Fluid also darkens with age.

When to change it: AAA's general guideline is about every two years, and it notes some makers say every two to three years. Your owner's manual has the interval for your car.

How to check it: the reservoir usually sits on top of the master cylinder at the back of the engine bay, on the driver's side. The level should be between the marks. New fluid is clear to tan; dark fluid is a sign it needs a service. Use only the type your manual names. Some makers, such as Tesla, tell owners not to top it up themselves, so check the manual first.

Warning signs: a level near or below the lower mark, or having to add fluid often, can mean a leak or worn pads. AAA advises having the brakes inspected as soon as possible. If the red brake warning light comes on while driving, brake gently and stop when it's safe.

Brake fluid damages paint, so wipe up spills right away.

Add a Brake fluid reminder in Checkpit and set it to repeat at your manual's interval.

Sources:
- AAA (Your AAA Network), How to Care for Your Car Brakes: https://magazine.northeast.aaa.com/daily/life/cars-trucks/care-for-car-brakes/
- AAA, Car Fluids: How to Check and Maintain Them: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/quick-tips-for-checking-vehicle-fluids
- Tesla, Model 3 Checking Brake Fluid: https://service.tesla.com/docs/Public/diy/model3/en_us/GUID-1D888517-65DF-4501-9F8A-90A7E879068F.html

posts.title: Car battery: how long it lasts and when to test it
posts.body:
Most car batteries last three to five years, according to both AAA and Australia's NRMA. Climate matters: AAA says a battery may last five years or more in cooler places but around three years in hot ones, because heat speeds up wear.

What shortens battery life:
- Mostly short trips, which don't let the battery fully recharge (NRMA adds that running the air conditioning or infotainment on those trips makes it harder)
- Long periods parked, since batteries slowly discharge
- A loose hold-down that lets the battery vibrate
- Letting it go completely flat, even if it's recharged afterward
- A fault in the charging system

Signs it may be failing: slow engine cranking, clicking when you turn the key, the battery or charging warning light, dim headlights at idle, frequent jump-starts, a rotten-egg smell, or a swollen case. Some batteries fail with no warning at all.

When to test: AAA suggests checking the battery and cable connections at every oil change and having the battery tested every year once it's three years old. NRMA also recommends a battery health check after three years. At about five years, a battery is near the end of its usual life.

Keep the terminals clean and tight and the hold-down secure. When replacing it, match the type, group number and CCA or Ah rating your vehicle calls for.

Log the battery's install date in Checkpit and add a Battery reminder for a yearly test from year three.

Sources:
- AAA, How Long Do Car Batteries Last: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/how-long-do-car-batteries-last
- AAA, When to Replace Your Car's Battery: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/when-to-replace-your-cars-battery
- NRMA, Taking care of your battery: https://www.mynrma.com.au/roadside-assistance/car-batteries/taking-care-of-your-battery

posts.title: Dashboard warning lights: what the colors mean
posts.body:
Most cars color-code their warning lights. Symbols vary, so your owner's manual is the final word; National Highways (England) suggests checking it or asking the maker about anything specific to your car.

Red: a possibly serious or dangerous problem. The RAC's advice is to stop as soon as it's safe and get the car checked.
Amber or yellow: something needs checking soon. Less urgent, but don't ignore it.
Green, white or blue: information only, such as a system being on.
National Highways advises not starting a trip with a red or amber light showing.

Lights that come on briefly when you start the car are normal. One that stays on is the one to act on.

Red lights to take seriously (RAC guidance):
- Brake: pull over safely, keep speed low and avoid sudden braking.
- Oil: stop when safe, switch off and check the oil level. If the level is fine, don't drive on; the pump may be at fault.
- Engine temperature: stop and let the engine cool before checking coolant.
- Battery or charging: the car may lose power suddenly, so get it checked.
- Airbag: the airbags may not work in a crash. Get it checked right away.

Amber lights: tire pressure (check pressures when safe), ABS on its own (normal braking should still work, but get it checked; with the brake light too, stop), and engine management (get it checked as soon as you can).

On a highway or motorway, don't stop in a live lane unless you must. If you can drive safely, head for the next exit or service area.

When a light leads to a repair, log it in Checkpit with the date and mileage.

Sources:
- RAC, Dashboard warning lights guide: https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/advice/know-how/car-dashboard-warning-lights-meaning/
- National Highways, Dashboard warning lights: what you need to know: https://nationalhighways.co.uk/road-safety/dashboard-warning-lights/

posts.title: Vehicle recalls: how to check if your car has one
posts.body:
A recall means the maker has found a safety problem with a vehicle or part. Checking is free and takes a few minutes.

Find your VIN: it's 17 characters. NHTSA says to look at the lower left of the windshield; it's also on your registration and may be on your insurance card.

US: enter your VIN at nhtsa.gov/recalls. It shows unrepaired recalls from about the past 15 years. NHTSA's free SaferCar app can alert you to new recalls for a vehicle you've saved.
Canada: Transport Canada's database lists recalls issued in Canada since 1970, and it suggests looking up your VIN on the maker's website. The Government of Canada recalls and safety alerts app also shows vehicle recalls.
UK: GOV.UK's recall check uses your registration number, or the make, model and year.
Australia: search the federal Vehicle Recalls website (vehiclerecalls.gov.au), where you can also sign up for email alerts.

Is the fix free? NHTSA tells owners to contact a dealer to fix the recalled part for free. Transport Canada says makers almost always repair recalls free of charge, and GOV.UK says you usually won't pay for repairs or parts.

Registering your car with the maker is one way to get recall notices directly, according to Transport Canada. GOV.UK says not to drive a vehicle with a serious safety defect.

After a recall repair, log it in Checkpit with the date and mileage so it stays in the car's history.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Check for Recalls: https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls
- Transport Canada, Stay informed about recalls of vehicles, tires and child car seats: https://tc.canada.ca/en/road-transportation/defects-recalls-vehicles-tires-child-car-seats/stay-informed-about-recalls-vehicles-tires-child-car-seats
- GOV.UK, Check if a vehicle, part or accessory has been recalled: https://www.gov.uk/check-vehicle-recall
- Australian Government, New home for Australian vehicle recalls: https://www.vehiclerecalls.gov.au/news/new-home-australian-vehicle-recalls

posts.title: Engine coolant: how to check it and when to look closer
posts.body:
Coolant (antifreeze) is mixed with water to keep the engine from overheating in summer and freezing in winter. It also protects the cooling system from rust and corrosion.

Check it cold. The AA says to wait at least 30 minutes after switching off, longer if the engine has overheated, and not to open the cap until the engine has fully cooled, because hot coolant is under pressure and can scald. Find the see-through expansion tank (your manual shows where it is). The level should be between the min and max marks. The AA suggests a quick look every couple of weeks.

Topping up: use only the coolant type your vehicle calls for. The AA notes that different types don't mix well, many need a 50/50 mix with water, and some makers use a pre-mixed coolant you shouldn't add anything to. Plain water is for emergencies only, since coolant that's too weak can freeze in winter. Never pour antifreeze into the washer, brake or power steering reservoirs.

When to look closer: the AA says modern cooling systems shouldn't need topping up between services, so a dropping level means a visit to a shop. Watch for wet or white stains on hoses, cool air from the heater on the hot setting, and the coolant warning light (amber usually means low level; red means overheating).

Replacing it: coolant turns acidic over time and loses its rust protection. AAA says that once a car reaches 75,000 miles, the coolant should be tested at regular intervals, and if the test is fine, no flush is needed. Your owner's manual has the replacement interval.

Add a Coolant reminder in Checkpit and log each test or change with the mileage.

Sources:
- The AA, How to check your engine coolant and top it up: https://www.theaa.com/breakdown-cover/advice/how-to-check-your-engine-coolant
- AAA, Do I Need to Do That Transmission, Coolant, Brake Fluid Flush?: https://mwg.aaa.com/automotive/auto-repair/articles/do-you-need-transmission-coolant-brake-fluid-flush

posts.title: Winter car checklist: what to check before the cold
posts.body:
Cold weather is hard on cars. Here is what NHTSA and Public Safety Canada (with the CAA) suggest checking before winter.

Battery: cold reduces battery power, and engines need more of it to start. NHTSA suggests having a mechanic check the battery, charging system and belts.

Tires: pressure drops as it gets colder. Check it at least once a month with the tires cold, and fill to the number on the driver's door label or in the manual, not the one on the tire. NHTSA says tread should be at least 2/32 inch on every tire, and to check the spare too. Winter tires add grip on cold roads.

Wipers and washer fluid: fill up with winter washer fluid (Public Safety Canada suggests one rated to -40°C, plus a spare jug), replace blades that streak, and make sure the defrosters work.

Coolant and lights: check the coolant level and that it meets the maker's specification, and look for leaks. Check headlights, brake lights, turn signals and hazard lights.

Fuel: NHTSA says to keep the tank close to full; Public Safety Canada says at least half full. For electric and hybrid cars, NHTSA suggests keeping the battery charged; plugging in overnight helps.

Emergency kit: ice scraper and snow brush, small shovel, sand or cat litter for traction, jumper cables, flashlight, warning lights or flares, blankets, first aid kit, water, snacks and a phone charger.

If you get stuck, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow and run the engine only now and then to stay warm, never for long with the windows up.

Log your pre-winter check in Checkpit and set reminders for battery tests and tire changes.

Sources:
- NHTSA, Winter Weather Driving Tips: https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips
- Public Safety Canada (with CAA), Winter Driving: https://getprepared.gc.ca/cnt/rsrcs/sfttps/tp201002-en.aspx

posts.title: Wiper blades and washer fluid: when to replace and refill
posts.body:
Clear glass is a safety basic, and in Great Britain it's a legal one too: GOV.UK says a car with a windscreen must have working automatic wipers and a washer, kept in efficient working order.

When to replace blades: AAA says most mechanics and makers recommend new blades every six to twelve months. Climate, where you park, how often you use them and the type of blade all affect how long they last.

Signs they're worn: streaks or smears that get in the way, squeaking, skipping across the glass (cold can harden the rubber), and cracked, torn or frayed rubber. Check the manual or measure the old blades to get the right size.

Washer fluid: before winter, NHTSA suggests filling the reservoir with winter de-icing fluid and checking the defrosters, and notes that heavy-duty winter blades help where snow and ice are common. Public Safety Canada suggests fluid rated to -40°C and carrying a spare jug.

Before a winter drive: the UK Highway Code (rule 229) says you must clear all snow and ice from every window and keep lights clean and number plates readable. It also says to clear the mirrors, demist the windows, and remove snow that could fall onto other road users.

Add a Wiper blades reminder in Checkpit for every 6 or 12 months.

Sources:
- AAA, How to Change Your Wiper Blades: https://www.acg.aaa.com/connect/blogs/5c/auto/how-to-change-your-wiper-blades
- NHTSA, Winter Weather Driving Tips: https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips
- Public Safety Canada (with CAA), Winter Driving: https://getprepared.gc.ca/cnt/rsrcs/sfttps/tp201002-en.aspx
- GOV.UK, Windscreen wipers and washers on road vehicles: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/windscreen-wipers-and-washers-on-road-vehicles/summary-of-the-requirements-for-windscreen-wipers-and-washers-on-road-vehicles
- GOV.UK, The Highway Code, Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237): https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-highway-code/driving-in-adverse-weather-conditions-226-to-237

posts.title: Engine air filter: when it really needs changing
posts.body:
The engine air filter keeps dirt out of the air your engine takes in.

Fuel economy: Oak Ridge National Laboratory tests for the US Department of Energy found that on modern fuel-injected cars, a clogged filter had no measurable effect on fuel economy but did slow acceleration. With a clean filter, full-throttle 20 to 80 mph times were 6% to 11% quicker. FuelEconomy.gov says only older carbureted engines (built until the early 1980s) gain a few percent in fuel economy from a new filter.

When to change it: AAA says most makers call for regular inspection, with replacement as needed or at a set mileage. In clean city or suburban driving, a filter may last 20,000 miles (about 32,000 km) or more; dusty roads call for more frequent changes. Your owner's manual has the interval for your car.

How to check: dirt you can see doesn't always mean it's worn out. AAA's test for pleated paper filters is to hold it up to a bright light; if more than half the light gets through, it can stay in. That test doesn't work for dense fabric "extended life" filters, so change those at the maker's interval unless they're visibly caked with dirt. Some pickups have an indicator on the filter housing to check at each oil change.

Changing the filter more often than needed costs money without a real benefit.

Add an Air filter reminder in Checkpit at your manual's interval and log each change with the mileage.

Sources:
- AAA, Changing Your Car's Engine Air Filter: https://www.aaa.com/autorepair/articles/changing-your-cars-engine-air-filter
- FuelEconomy.gov, Keeping Your Vehicle in Shape: https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/maintain.jsp
- U.S. Department of Energy, Fact #568: For Modern Cars, Replacing an Air Filter Will Improve Performance but Not Fuel Economy: https://www.energy.gov/eere/vehicles/fact-568-april-27-2009-modern-cars-replacing-air-filter-will-improve-performance-not
